content:
**Subject and central claims.** This section of Steven Pinker's *Learnability and Cognition* continues Chapter 4's analysis of verb alternations, moving from causative verbs to passivizable verbs. Pinker argues that argument structure is a projection of "thematic cores," and that the syntactic form of a construction, its interpretive effect, and its verb selectivity all follow from one principle (file page 178). For causative alternations, he distinguishes two motivations: some verbs resist causativization because their meanings involve inherent internal causes (emission, disappearance) that cannot be directly caused from outside, while others resist stem-sharing (kill/die, bring/come) not because conflation is impossible but because narrow-range lexical rules determine whether a verb root may be bent to cover both meanings (file page 177). A cross-linguistic survey by Nedyalkov and Silnitsky suggests a universal continuum of "lexical causativizability," from human actions to simple state changes, with emission and disappearance verbs in between; no language lexicalizes "cause to laugh," while break commonly alternates (file page 178).

**Passive: the opposite problem.** Unlike the dative, causative, and locative alternations, where broad-range thematic cores overgenerate and narrow-range rules must restrict, the passive undergenerates semantically: all clear agent-patient verbs passivize, but many verbs without obvious agents or patients also passivize (receive, open with instrument subject, surround but not contain, own but not have) (file pages 178–179). Pinker says no existing theory fully demarcates these boundaries (file page 180). His proposal: the broad-range passive rule applies productively to all and only transitive verbs with agent and patient roles, supplying a sufficient condition; other verbs passivize only in versions where an agent-patient reading is available, whether by lexical ambiguity or by rules converting nonagentive forms into agentive ones (file page 180). Patient is understood abstractly, not only physically (file page 180).

**Force dynamics and abstract roles.** Drawing on Talmy, Pinker describes a force-dynamic model: agonists have inherent tendencies toward motion or rest; antagonists impose counteracting forces; causation can be steady-state, onset, or permissive ("letting"), and extends beyond physics to intrapsychic, social, and epistemic domains (file pages 182–183). Agents are antagonists with volitional intrinsic tendency; patients map to agonists, agents to antagonists (file pages 183–184). This lets abstract verbs like justify, nullify, prove, and create carry generalized agent-patient structure and hence passivize (file pages 184–185).

**Narrow rules and causal chains.** Instrumental subjects passivize only when the instrument is an intermediary link in a causal chain (a key opening a door), not a mere facilitator (a spoon eating cereal); Pinker posits an "intermediary instrument promotion" rule (file page 184). Similarly, "epistemic agent disembodiment" converts animate-agent verbs into abstract-subject versions whose content exerts force (file pages 184–185). Psych-verbs (please/frighten vs. like/fear) both passivize, posing a puzzle for role-to-function mapping that the section leaves unresolved at its end (file page 185).

**Limits.** Pinker concedes he cannot rule out a purely narrow-rule account of the passive and admits no theory fully captures the boundaries (file page 180). The continuum of causativizability is speculative ("one can speculate," file page 178). These are English verb-lexicon results, not universal learning laws.

**Engineering implications (mine, not Pinker's).** For a thinking machine, this suggests representing events as structured causal chains with typed roles (agonist/antagonist, patient/agent, instrument, experiencer), plus a distinction between broad-range schemas and narrow-range licensing rules that decide which instances may share a root or construction. A memory of past observations could tag events with force-dynamic profiles (onset, steady-state, permissive) and causal grain size, supporting analogical transfer and constrained generalization. The unresolved psych-verb cases warn that role-to-surface mappings may need multiple competing construals rather than a single deterministic rule. Nothing here demonstrates human-level intelligence or consciousness; it is a lexical-semantics analysis.
